newsitem.title: USA: Fed needs active role in bank regulation -- Meyer.
newsitem.headline: Fed needs active role in bank regulation -- Meyer.

text.p: As Congress considers changes to modernize banking that may shift powers among regulators, it is vital for the U.S. central bank to retain a hands-on supervisory role, Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said on Friday.

"That role is especially critical for large, global banking organizations but also for at least a cross-section of smaller banks," Meyer said in a speech prepared for delivery to a banking conference in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico.
A text of his remarks was issued in Washington.
"The Federal Reserve believes that such an active supervisory role is essential for it to conduct monetary policy and prevent or manage financial crises most effectively," Meyer said.

He cited the example of the "credit crunch" in the early 1990s, saying information that Fed examiners discovered about banks' reluctance to lend "contributed to the Federal Reserve's decision to maintain an unusually stimulative monetary policy well into the current expansion."
That supported the economy while banks regained their health so they could resume expanded lending, Meyer said.
"If there is consolidated regulation, it could be carried out by the Federal Reserve, in line with the system's current role as regulator of bank holding companies," Meyer said.

He said the Fed "has critical responsibilities to prevent or resolve major problems in financial markets," so it needs detailed knowledge of risk-management procedures and financial exposure of banks that regulation provides, Meyer said.

Financial services are moving in the direction of broader activities and more competition "with or without Congressional action" because of global competition and financial and technological innovations.
But Meyer said Congress' approval was needed for a clean move to modernize by ending limits on permitted activities for banking, securities and other financial services firms.
He said there was a growing consensus that selling all types of insurance and possibly underwriting life insurance presented no undue risks to banks and would help consumers.
